sections.title: Folding Complex Shapes (Triangle, Hexagon, Octagon)
sections.content: In Level 3, the paper may not be a square. It can be an equilateral triangle, hexagon, or octagon. These shapes have multiple lines of symmetry. When folded along one symmetry line, layers may not overlap evenly in all regions. You must carefully track which sections overlap and how many layers exist in each region.

sections.title: Overlapping and Uneven Folds
sections.content: Some folds create uneven overlapping. For example, folding all four corners of a square toward the center (envelope fold) creates more layers in the middle and fewer at the edges. Similarly, folding only one-third of the paper results in partial overlap. Different zones of the paper will have different numbers of layers.

sections.title: Complex Cutting on Partial Layers
sections.content: If a cut is made in a region where all layers overlap, the number of final shapes equals the total layers. However, if a cut is made on an edge where only some layers overlap, the number of final shapes equals only the layers present in that region. Therefore, total folds do not always determine the final count.

sections.title: Exact Count and Orientation Analysis
sections.content: Options may specify exact counts and directions, such as: '12 triangles are formed, 6 pointing toward the center and 6 pointing outward.' You must determine not only how many shapes form, but also how they rotate and face after unfolding.

sections.title: 4–6 Step Solution Method
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the original shape and its symmetry lines. Step 2: After each fold, mentally divide the paper into zones (center, edge, corner) and count layers in each zone. Step 3: Identify where the cut is made and how many layers overlap at that location. Step 4: Multiply the cut only by the layers present in that specific zone. Step 5: Apply rotation and symmetry while unfolding. Step 6: Count inward and outward orientations separately and match with the options.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Assuming equal layers everywhere. 2. Multiplying cuts by total folds instead of local layers. 3. Ignoring rotation angles (60°, 90°, etc.). 4. Not separating inward and outward facing shapes.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Level 3 requires zone-wise layer tracking, careful observation of overlap, and accurate rotation analysis. Always count layers in the exact region of the cut and verify both total number and orientation of final shapes.

tricks.title: Symmetry Line Mapping
tricks.explanation: First identify all symmetry lines of the original shape.
tricks.example: A hexagon may produce 6 repeated shapes after full unfolding.

tricks.title: Zone-Wise Layer Counting
tricks.explanation: Divide the folded paper into zones and count layers separately.
tricks.example: Center = 4 layers, edge = 2 layers, corner = 1 layer.

tricks.title: Local Layer Rule
tricks.explanation: Multiply cuts only by the number of overlapping layers in that region.
tricks.example: If only 3 layers overlap at the edge, only 3 shapes form.

tricks.title: Rotation Tracking Trick
tricks.explanation: Visualize how shapes rotate when unfolded.
tricks.example: In a triangle fold, shapes may rotate by 60°.

tricks.title: Envelope Fold Analysis
tricks.explanation: When corners are folded inward, the center has maximum layers.
tricks.example: Four corners folded → center may have 4 layers.

tricks.title: Inward-Outward Separation
tricks.explanation: Count inward-facing and outward-facing shapes separately.

tricks.title: Edge-Specific Cut Awareness
tricks.explanation: Cuts on partial overlap edges produce fewer shapes.
tricks.example: 8 total folds but only 4 layers at that edge → 4 shapes.

tricks.title: 6-Step Mental Flow
tricks.explanation: Identify shape → Mark symmetry → Count zone layers → Locate cut → Apply rotation → Final exact count.
tricks.example: Hexagon + uneven fold + edge cut → count layers in edge zone before multiplying.
